title: Encore - What is it like to be face blind? With Joe DeGutis, PhD, and Sadie Dingfelder

sentences.en: Speaking of psychology is taking a summer break, so we're rerunning some of our favorite episodes from the paSt. Back in 2021, I talked to psychologist Joe DeGudis and journalist
sentences.zh: 《心理学话题》正在过暑假，因此我们将重播过去一些最受欢迎的节目。早在2021年，我曾与心理学家乔·德古蒂斯以及记者

sentences.en: Sadie Dingfelder, author of a new book about what it's like to be face-blind, about what scientists are learning about prozopagnosia or face-blindness.
sentences.zh: 萨迪·丁芬德勒（她写了一本关于面孔失认症体验的新书）进行了交谈，探讨了科学家对面孔失认症（又称脸盲症）的新发现。

sentences.en: We hope you enjoyed this episode from the archives.
sentences.zh: 希望大家喜欢这期来自档案库的节目。

sentences.en: Speaking of psychology, we'll be back with new episodes in late AuguSt. Thank you for listening.
sentences.zh: 说到《心理学话题》，我们将在八月下旬携全新节目回归。谢谢收听。

sentences.en: Imagine living in a world where everyone looks vaguely familiar, but you never know for certain exactly who anyone is.
sentences.zh: 想象一下，生活在一个这样的世界里：每个人看起来都有点面熟，但你永远无法确定具体是谁。

sentences.en: Your old classmates, your coworkers, your friends, and even your family members all can appear at first glance to be friendly strangers who seem to know you.
sentences.zh: 你的老同学、同事、朋友，甚至家人，初看之下都像是那些似乎认识你的友好陌生人。

sentences.en: That's what life is like for people with prozopagnosia or face-blindness.
sentences.zh: 这就是患有面孔失认症（即脸盲症）的人的生活写照。

sentences.en: Historically, the disorder was thought to be rare, but more recent research suggests it may affect as many as one in 50 people.
sentences.zh: 从历史上看，人们曾认为这种障碍很罕见，但最新的研究表明，多达五十分之一的人可能会受其影响。

sentences.en: Last year, Sadie Dingfelder found out she was one of them.
sentences.zh: 去年，萨迪·丁芬德勒发现自己就是其中之一。

sentences.en: Sadie is a former colleague of mine.
sentences.zh: 萨迪是我的前同事。

sentences.en: She used to be an editor at APA's magazine, and I later hired her to be editor of our website.
sentences.zh: 她曾是美国心理协会杂志的编辑，后来我聘请她担任我们网站的编辑。

sentences.en: After a lifetime of thinking that there was something just a little bit different about her brain,
sentences.zh: 在经历了一生都觉得自己大脑有点与众不同之后，

sentences.en: Sadie took part in a study at Harvard Medical School that finally gave her some clarity about her condition.
sentences.zh: 萨迪参加了哈佛医学院的一项研究，这终于让她对自己的病情有了清晰的认识。

sentences.en: She wrote about the experience for the Washington Post magazine.
sentences.zh: 她为《华盛顿邮报》杂志撰文记录了这段经历。

sentences.en: So what is it like to have prozopagnosia?
sentences.zh: 那么，患有面孔失认症是怎样的体验？

sentences.en: And what have psychologists and other scientists learned about the causes of face-blindness?
sentences.zh: 心理学家和其他科学家对脸盲症的成因有了哪些了解？

sentences.en: Can it be treated?
sentences.zh: 它能被治疗吗？

sentences.en: If so, how?
sentences.zh: 如果可以，怎么治？

sentences.en: Joining Sadie and me is Dr. Joseph Dugudis, a neuroscientist and experimental psychologist at Harvard Medical School and the Boston VA.
sentences.zh: 与萨迪和我一同做客的是约瑟夫·德古蒂斯博士，他是哈佛医学院和波士顿退伍军人事务医疗系统的神经科学家兼实验心理学家。

sentences.en: He studies the neuroscience of face blindness and has developed treatment programs to help those with face blindness improve their ability to recognize faces.
sentences.zh: 他研究脸盲症的神经科学，并开发了治疗项目，以帮助脸盲症患者提高识别面孔的能力。

sentences.en: He runs the study that Sadie participated in and was the person who confirmed her self-diagnosis.
sentences.zh: 他负责萨迪参加的那项研究，也是证实她自我诊断的人。

sentences.en: Welcome to Speaking of Psychology.
sentences.zh: 欢迎来到《心理学话题》。

sentences.en: Thanks.
sentences.zh: 谢谢。

sentences.en: Thanks for having me.
sentences.zh: 谢谢邀请我来。

sentences.en: Yeah.
sentences.zh: 好。

sentences.en: Sadie, let's start with the question that I posed in the intro.
sentences.zh: 萨迪，让我们从我在开场白中提出的问题开始。

sentences.en: What is it like to have prosopagnosia?
sentences.zh: 患有面孔失认症是怎样的体验？

sentences.en: When you look at people, what do you see?
sentences.zh: 当你看着别人时，你看到了什么？

sentences.en: Yeah, well, a lot of people think that face blind people maybe just see a blur where faces, that's definitely not true.
sentences.zh: 嗯，很多人认为脸盲症患者看面孔时可能只看到一片模糊，这绝对不是真的。

sentences.en: I have good visual acuity.
sentences.zh: 我的视力很好。

sentences.en: My problem is I just don't remember faces.
sentences.zh: 我的问题是我根本记不住面孔。

sentences.en: Like the second I'm looking away from them, they're gone from my memory.
sentences.zh: 就像我把视线从他们身上移开的那一秒，他们就在我的记忆中消失了。

sentences.en: And I was kind of astounded to find out that everyone else has like an almost photographic visual memory for faces specifically.
sentences.zh: 当我发现其他人对人脸竟然有着近乎照片般的视觉记忆时，我感到相当震惊。

sentences.en: Dr. Dugutis, what does the research tell us about why prosopagnosics can't do this thing that other people do so effortlessly, recognizing and remembering faces?
sentences.zh: 德古蒂斯博士，研究告诉我们，为什么脸盲症患者无法做到其他人那样毫不费力的事情——识别和记住面孔？

sentences.en: Is the problem memory, perception, or perhaps both?
sentences.zh: 问题出在记忆、感知，还是两者兼有？

sentences.en: Yeah, that's a great question.
sentences.zh: 是的，这是一个很好的问题。

sentences.en: I think that the research shows right now in our kind of recent results have found kind of two different maybe subtypes.
sentences.zh: 我认为目前的研究表明，根据我们最近的结果，可能存在两种不同的亚型。

sentences.en: So one, more of a perceptual subtype where you can't tell faces apart that are right in front
sentences.zh: 一种是更偏向感知层面的亚型，你无法分辨就在你眼前的

sentences.en: of you, and then there's also this more of this memory component where, you know, the kind
sentences.zh: 不同面孔；另一种则是更偏向记忆组件的亚型，你知道的，正如

sentences.en: of like you were saying in the intro, prosopagnosics can have this vague kind of feeling, but they
sentences.zh: 你在开场白中所说，脸盲症患者可能会有一种模糊的感觉，但

sentences.en: don't have this kind of rich, robust kind of once they see somebody where all this other information about the person comes back to them automatically.
sentences.zh: 一旦他们看到某人，他们不会拥那种丰富、强健的体验，即关于这个人的所有其他信息会自动涌回脑海。

sentences.en: And, you know, people are remarkably good at faces.
sentences.zh: 而且，你知道，人类辨别面孔的能力非常惊人。

sentences.en: And I think that this is one of the things that it could be, you know, from an evolutionary
sentences.zh: 我认为从演化的角度来看，这可能是其中原因之一，

sentences.en: standpoint, it looks like, you know, the face may be exploded in the genetic kind of variation.
sentences.zh: 看起来人脸在基因变异方面似乎呈爆发式增长。

sentences.en: And in some ways, I think a lot of, you know, we capitalize on this and we are able to kind
sentences.zh: 在某种程度上，我认为我们很多人都利用了这一点，并能够通过面孔来识别个体，嗯，

sentences.en: of recognize individuals by their faces and, um, in other species, like for instance, penguins, they don't have quite a, you know, maybe people are like, well, if I were a penguin,
sentences.zh: 而在其他物种中，比如企鹅，它们的脸没有……嗯，也许人们会想，“如果我是企鹅，

sentences.en: I could recognize penguin faces, but their faces don't, they don't vary as much.
sentences.zh: 我就能认出企鹅的脸”，但它们的脸并没有那么多变。

sentences.en: So the human face is exploded in, in variability and, you know, our brains have, have kind of, um, maybe evolved to capitalize on that.
sentences.zh: 因此，人脸在变异性上呈爆发式增长，而我们的大脑也已经演化得能够充分利用这一点。

sentences.en: Uh, and I think with prosopagnosics, yeah, there's these very subtle, um, deficits that maybe accumulate and, uh, they're not able to capitalize on all this variability.
sentences.zh: 嗯，我认为对于脸盲症患者来说，确实存在这些非常微妙的缺陷，可能会累积起来，导致他们无法利用所有这些变异性。

sentences.en: And the, one of the remarkable things too, I want to just say is that it's a pretty specific disorder.
sentences.zh: 而且，我还想说的一个显著特点是，这是一种非常具体的障碍。

sentences.en: I think we keep as scientists, we see that, um, these people are, you know, have, have normal in, in sometimes above average, like intellectual abilities and other abilities.
sentences.zh: 作为科学家，我们不断发现，这些人具有正常、有时甚至高于平均水平的智力能力和其他能力。

sentences.en: Um, so it's like one of these developmental disorders that's very, seems pretty, like very specific, you know, um, in comparison to other developmental disorders.
sentences.zh: 因此，与其它发展性障碍相比，它似乎是一种非常特定、非常明确的发展性障碍。

sentences.en: So it seems like this vision and visual memory, uh, specific disorder.
sentences.zh: 所以这似乎是一种专门针对视觉和视觉记忆的障碍。

sentences.en: What's actually happening in brains like Sadie's when they see people's faces?
sentences.zh: 当萨迪这样的人看到别人的脸时，他们的大脑里究竟发生了什么？

sentences.en: What have you learned from brain imaging studies about where this disorder originates in the brain?
sentences.zh: 从脑成像研究中，你了解到这种障碍究竟源于大脑的哪个部位？

sentences.en: Yeah.
sentences.zh: 是的。

sentences.en: So I think one of the things that we're finding is that there's kind of these two, uh, uh, perceptual processes.
sentences.zh: 所以我想我们发现的一点是，存在着这两种感知过程。

sentences.en: And I know, I know Sadie's results, so I'm not going to, I'm not going to totally go into her results, but, but basically a lot of prosopagnosics, um, have trouble with putting
sentences.zh: 我知道萨迪的检测结果，所以我不会完全透露她的结果，但基本上，很多脸盲症患者在将面孔的所有部分组合成一个完整的整体时

sentences.en: all the parts of the face together into a, a complete whole.
sentences.zh: 会遇到困难。

sentences.en: So this is something we do automatically.
sentences.zh: 所以这是我们自动完成的事情。

sentences.en: You can call it a holistic processing or gestalt processing.
sentences.zh: 你可以称之为整体加工或格式塔加工。

sentences.en: And it's, it's something that is very fast and automatic.
sentences.zh: 这是非常迅速且自动化的过程。

sentences.en: Uh, the other thing that we're finding is that a lot of the prosopagnosics have particular trouble with, uh, kind of being sensitive to the eye region.
sentences.zh: 另一件我们发现的事情是，许多脸盲症患者在对眼部区域保持敏感方面存在特殊困难。

sentences.en: So the eyes hold, hold a lot of information with regard to identity.
sentences.zh: 因此，眼睛包含了大量关于身份的信息。

sentences.en: So that's something that, um, you know, one of the main mechanisms of like these kind of
sentences.zh: 所以，这些感知缺陷的主要机制之一，

sentences.en: perceptual deficits are both maybe a combination of these feature, uh, lack of feature sensitivity, and then a difficulty with putting the, the face together into a whole.
sentences.zh: 要么是缺乏特征敏感性的组合，要么是难以将面孔组合成一个整体。

sentences.en: Um, so that's on the, on the perceptual side of things.
sentences.zh: 嗯，所以在感知方面就是这样。

sentences.en: And, um, and then on the, more on the memory side, I kind of, um, it's, it's kind of this, this type of memory that we call recollection memory.
sentences.zh: 然后，在记忆方面，我想……这是一种我们称之为回忆记忆的记忆类型。

sentences.en: So, uh, recollection memory, again, it's like kind of taking a face and making all these associations with all this other information.
sentences.zh: 因此，回忆记忆同样是将一张面孔提取出来，并与所有其他信息建立起种种关联。

sentences.en: And usually when you see a face, all this extra, uh, semantic information, like their name, their job, when you last saw them comes flooding back without any effort.
sentences.zh: 通常当你看到一张脸时，所有这些额外的语义信息，比如他们的名字、工作、你上次见到他们是什么时候，都会不费吹灰之力地涌现出来。

sentences.en: Now, when a prosopagnosic, and I think Sadie can say more about this, sees a face, they don't get this flood of, of information.
sentences.zh: 现在，当脸盲症患者（我想萨迪可以对此多说一点）看到一张脸时，他们不会获得这种信息的涌入。

sentences.en: A lot of times they're, they're, um, they're met with this kind of vague sense of, of, of knowing, and we call that, you know, familiarity memory.
sentences.zh: 很多时候，他们迎来的只是一种模糊的“认识”感，我们称之为熟悉感记忆。

sentences.en: Um, and sometime, and that was kind of coined back in the eighties as the butcher on the bus phenomenon.
sentences.zh: 嗯，有时，这个概念在80年代被称为“公车上的屠夫”现象。

sentences.en: When you see somebody out of context, um, let's say you're a butcher or a barista that you frequent and you can't place who it is now.
sentences.zh: 当你打破常规场景看到某人时，比方说一个你经常光顾的屠夫或咖啡师，而你现在想不起他是谁。

sentences.en: Prosopagnosics, I'd love to hear more of what Sadie says.
sentences.zh: 对于脸盲症患者，我很想听听萨迪更多的看法。

sentences.en: It, it, this happens, this might happen with very, very familiar people.
sentences.zh: 这种情况甚至可能发生在非常非常熟悉的人身上。

sentences.en: Um, whereas in, with people who don't have prosopagnosia, this may just happen with a new acquaintance.
sentences.zh: 而在没有面孔失认症的人身上，这可能只会发生在新的熟人身上。

sentences.en: Does this happen to you, Sadie?
sentences.zh: 萨迪，你也有这种情况吗？

sentences.en: Do, do you have a butcher on the bus?
sentences.zh: 你、你也有公车上的屠夫吗？

sentences.en: Oh yeah.
sentences.zh: 哦，是的。

sentences.en: I, I have, I have a lot of trouble, um, uh, identifying people out of context.
sentences.zh: 我、我在打破常规场景时辨认认出人方面有很大困难。

sentences.en: Um, but I have a lot of trouble identifying people who are right in their normal context too.
sentences.zh: 不过，我在正常场景下辨认人也有很大困难。

sentences.en: Um, I was just on the elevator in my apartment, in my apartment building.
sentences.zh: 我刚才在我的公寓大楼的电梯里，

sentences.en: And, um, this woman was like, oh, Hey Sadie.
sentences.zh: 然后，有个女人说：“哦，嘿，萨迪。”

sentences.en: And I had no idea who she was.
sentences.zh: 我根本不知道她是谁。

sentences.en: We were both wearing masks.
sentences.zh: 我们俩都戴着口罩。

sentences.en: And I'm like, I'm sorry, I have no idea who you are.
sentences.zh: 我说：“对不起，我完全不知道你是谁。”

sentences.en: And she's like, oh, I cat sat for you like last week.
sentences.zh: 她说：“哦，我上周还帮你喂过猫呢。”

sentences.en: And I was like, oh, cool.
sentences.zh: 我说：“哦，酷。”

sentences.en: So, um, yeah, she was in my building and I could, did not recognize her, but the masks make it really hard.
sentences.zh: 所以，嗯，她就住在我的大楼里，但我认不出她，不过口罩确实让这变得很难。

sentences.en: That, that has to be tough.
sentences.zh: 那一定很艰难。

sentences.en: Not only for people like Sadie, but what happens to, uh, children at various levels of development.
sentences.zh: 不仅对萨迪这样的人来说如此，处于各个发展阶段的儿童又会发生什么呢？

sentences.en: I mean, if we're going around wearing masks for the next year or more, Dr. Dugutis, is that going to have any effect on their development?
sentences.zh: 我的意思是，如果我们接下来一年或更长时间都要戴着口罩出门，德古蒂斯博士，你认为这会对他们的发育产生任何影响吗？

sentences.en: Do you think?
sentences.zh: 你觉得呢？

sentences.en: You know, I don't think we know, but I mean, I think that the, um, uh, you know, the face recognition system needs to have a lot of input and a lot of different faces.
sentences.zh: 你知道，我想我们还不知道，但我的意思是，嗯……人脸识别系统需要大量的输入和许多不同的面孔。

sentences.en: And actually they found that some people that grow up in kind of smaller towns, even, you know, may not be as good at face recognition than people who grew up in larger cities that
sentences.zh: 事实上，研究发现，在较小城镇长大的一些人，甚至可能不如在能够接触到更多面孔的大城市长大的人擅长人脸识别。

sentences.en: have more exposure.
sentences.zh: 有证据表明，人脸识别可能存在某些关键期，

sentences.en: And there's a little bit, there's some evidence that there may be these kinds of critical
sentences.zh: 在这些时期里，嗯……也许你能区分所有面孔。

sentences.en: periods, uh, for face recognition where you, um, uh, you know, maybe you can differentiate, um, all faces.
sentences.zh: 这与所谓的“异族效应”有关，即你可能能够区分所有不同族裔的面孔。

sentences.en: And this is something called like related to the other race effect where you may be able to differentiate all faces of all different ethnicities.
sentences.zh: 过了一段时间后，你接触最多的那个族裔，你在那方面的识别能力就会变得更好。

sentences.en: And then after a while you're, you, you kind of, whatever ethnicity you're most exposed to, you get better at that.
sentences.zh: 所以，可能存在这些关键期。

sentences.en: Um, so there may be these critical periods.
sentences.zh: 我希望……我认为这是一个有趣的问题，这是否正在影响发育，或者我们是否可以依靠神经可塑性，即大脑重新组织和恢复的能力。

sentences.en: I, I hope, um, I think it's an interesting question if this is affecting development or if, or if we can kind of rely on, you know, neuroplasticity or the ability for the brain
sentences.zh: 但我确实认为，仅看到部分面孔可能会破坏这种整体加工过程，以及将整张脸组合在一起的能力。

sentences.en: to kind of, uh, reorganize and recover.
sentences.zh: 所以，确实有可能。

sentences.en: But I do think just seeing, you know, part of the face may disrupt this holistic processing and kind of putting all the face together.
sentences.zh: 我想知道，嗯……就像所有的孩子都在玩TikTok，对吧？

sentences.en: Um, so it could.
sentences.zh: 我在想，接触屏幕上扁平化的面孔是否能弥补这一点。

sentences.en: I wonder if, um, like all the kids are on TikTok, right?
sentences.zh: 我想我们需要做研究。

sentences.en: I wonder if, um, exposure to faces that are flattened on a screen is like, can make up for it.
sentences.zh: 问你这个问题其实很不公平，德古蒂斯博士，因为你不是发展心理学家。
